premise:
Document (publication date: 1928-02-17): Johann Heinrich Pestalozzi.
Already a year separates us from the commemorations of Pestalozzi's 100th anniversary of death, which had so much to say to our generation that was timely. In our self-centered age, they presented the man who overcame himself a hundredfold and loved boundlessly. They preached from the sanctuary of the hearth, from the blessing of the family, as if Pestalozzi could have foreseen our dissolution of the family. And they showed the invincibility of a good will and a pure heart as a visible reality.

How gladly, even after a year, one surveys the life and work of this man once more and, under qualified guidance—such as the modest yet significant little book by Prof. Dr. F. Medicus*—wanders contemplatively through it like a garden! One encounters Heiri Wunderli of Thorlikon, the fatherless orphan under the domestic rule of women. The influence of the grandfathers, both friends of the people—Bodmer, Rousseau—the patriots, especially Bluntschli, makes itself felt. Anna Schultheß comes into his life. "The letters exchanged between Pestalozzi and his fiancée mark the beginning of a tragedy..." Pure love moves into the boundless; no limit holds as ultimately valid for it. Where it appears as love between bridegroom and bride, it is nevertheless not confined to these two people: if it were, it would be selfish. Pure love loves the infinite in the beloved, and the infinite is all-encompassing."

Pestalozzi becomes a husband. "After long, hard struggles, the lovers were finally united. But a happy marriage was not granted to them. Very soon they had to experience that they were a heavy burden to each other." He becomes a father, a father to the poor, runs into misfortune, is doubted by relatives, even by his wife. "Only a few friends who knew his great heart did not give up on him." He lives the evening hour of a hermit. "The purely human must be cultivated, and even in the lowliest hut, this cultivation should not be lacking."

A glimmer of light: *Lienhard and Gertrud* is written. For a long time, Arner interested him most. For a time, the schoolmaster. Today, Gertrud has the most important things to say to us. He wrestles out the work on legislation and infanticide, which only became fully understandable in our century. "Society sits in judgment over sins that have been committed by itself, and which it avenges on its unfortunate victims."

Judging by his Swiss writings, what did not ferment in this mind! He carried the later erupting revolution first within himself. Stans greets him, burning for activity and proof of his worth. From the village schoolmaster at Schloßberg, he rises to become the seminary director at Burgdorf Castle. "His endeavor was to recognize the paths on which pedagogical work—not only his own, but any—must advance. He believed in the unalterable equality of human nature and in the eternity of human goals; and therefore he believed that a method of education must be the right, the necessary one." Even if his individual insights have little more to say to us today, his grounding of pedagogy in psychology, his principle of work—they live on. Pastor Niederer appears in his life circle. Are the two like Socrates and Plato, like Luther and Melanchthon, or like giver and—judge?

Via Münchenbuchsee, it goes to Yverdon. The gray castle walls there strike a sad note. There, between his 60th and 80th year, Pestalozzi became mortally ill in soul. Yet another little light: the school for the poor! A sorrow: the death of his wife! "At the funeral service, he held a moving dialogue with the deceased before the open coffin, now addressing her, now answering in her name. The thought of bearing the guilt for the misfortune of her life contended in him with the other, that his faithfulness to his holy calling had made the sacrifices brought by her necessary. A Bible, which he pressed to her breast, was the symbol of both spouses' superiority over every distress." A heavy declaration closes his institution: "I hope the public shares my pain that I find myself compelled to declare my projected foundation, from which I promised myself so much blessing..., as completely thwarted and myself as entirely incapable of really fulfilling the obligations which I undertook in this matter with so much devotion and sacrifice."

Then he goes home, back to the Neuhof. Through renewed sadness, the gate of death suddenly opens. He was!—Man, Christian, citizen, everything for others, nothing for himself.

That our time, like a thousand-voiced choir, paid homage to his name, that it mustered understanding for Pestalozzi, does it credit. Whether it will truly hear his life's sermon, however, cannot yet be decided after a year. Em.

premise:
Document (publication date: 1948-12-30): Nokrashy Pasha
No. 7. The Egyptian Prime Minister Mahmoud Fahmy El-Nokrashy Pasha, who was assassinated in Cairo on Monday, belonged, although he was already 60 years old, to the relatively young politicians who only entered the political arena in the last two decades. A former supporter of the Wafd, like virtually all Egyptian politicians, he first came to the fore as Minister of Transport in the second cabinet of Nahas Pasha, which remained in office only from January to June 1930. He held the same office again in the third Nahas cabinet from May 1936. His lively personality made him particularly popular among the young adherents of the party and also brought him closer to his party friend and contemporary Ahmed Maher Pasha, the President of the Chamber of Deputies, from whom he subsequently never parted.

Their parallel careers began in London, when they were both among the thirteen delegates who signed the Anglo-Egyptian treaty in August 1936. After their return to Egypt, they, as younger members of the party, gained the impression that the Wafd had played its last cards in London and thus had no more prospects to offer its followers. This viewpoint was entirely justified at the time; indeed, the actual decline of the Wafd began at that point. For when the Wafd was founded, the sole aim of its program was the conclusion of a treaty with Great Britain that would recognize Egypt's independence. It is known that the Arabic word "Wafd" means nothing other than "Delegation." This treaty was now wrested from the British by Nahas Pasha. The role of the Wafd "Delegation" was thus played out.

In the following months, the leaders of the party, primarily Makram Ebeid and to a lesser extent Nahas, behaved as if they now had a right to the country's lasting gratitude. Squandering of public funds, corruption, and favoritism became widespread. It was managed as if all hope had been abandoned of ever coming to power again later.

In August 1937, the two friends Maher and Nokrashy broke away from the Wafd and together founded a new party, which they named the Saadist Party after the founder of the Wafd, Saad Zaghloul, under the pretext that the party founded by him had not remained true to his spirit. The beginnings were difficult. The new party, however, ultimately prevailed, and when in August 1939 Ali Maher Pasha, the brother of Ahmed, needed their support in forming a new cabinet, he offered its president, Nokrashy, the Ministry of Education.

In June 1940, Ali Maher had to resign due to his pro-Axis leanings under pressure from the British embassy, and Nokrashy was taken over by the Hassan Sabry Pasha cabinet as Minister of the Interior. This extremely important office in wartime could undoubtedly only be entrusted to him in agreement with the English.

The Sabry cabinet remained at the helm for only two months. During the opening of parliament, the prime minister was struck by a heart attack while reading the throne speech. His successor, Hussein Sirry, dispensed with the participation of the Saadists. In February 1942, the Hussein Sirry cabinet was replaced by the last Wafd cabinet under Nahas Pasha. When in October 1944 Lord Killearn and the British government finally had to realize that Nahas Pasha's continued presence in the government endangered their own position, they withdrew their support from him and pressed for the appointment of Ahmed Maher Pasha as his successor, who, as an opponent of Nahas and a pro-British minded politician, was well-regarded both in the palace and at the British embassy. The two Saadist leaders had thereby reached the highest level; they divided the key positions between themselves. Maher kept the Ministry of the Interior for himself, and Nokrashy became Foreign Minister. Thus he had completed the second grade of the "prime ministerial school," for it has almost become a tradition in Egypt that the prime minister, unless he has reached his post via the presidency of the Senate or the Chamber, must have administered one of the three main ministries, namely the Interior, Foreign, or Finance Ministry.

Under Ahmed Maher's leadership, Egyptian policy was steered into British waters. Maher had to pay for this policy with his life after only a few months. Maher Pasha was shot dead on February 24, 1945, by a fanatical nationalist just as he was announcing to parliament Egypt's declaration of war on the Axis powers. For Nokrashy, under such circumstances, it was a difficult task to assume the succession of his friend. After the war, nationalism intensified in Egypt, which Nokrashy attempted to counter. As a realist politician who understood how to accurately assess the power resources of his country, he believed he could wrest concessions from the British through friendship, which they would never grant to declared enemies. Personally, Nokrashy would have gladly done without a revision of the London treaty, clearly recognizing that provisions and clauses only have value if one can force the partner to fulfill its obligations through appropriate means. However, he had to yield to the pressure of the "Eighteen," an advisory committee that the king had brought into being. When he wanted to begin negotiations with London, his government had to give way to the machinations of the opposition. Nokrashy lacked the necessary self-control and calm. This was also evident when in February 1946 he ordered the police to ruthlessly shoot at unarmed student crowds who wanted to cross the Abbas Bridge into the government district. His brutal course of action betrayed not energy, but rather fear.

After Nokrashy Pasha's resignation on February 15, 1946, Ismail Sidky Pasha took over the cabinet, which was supported by Nokrashy, but already had to resign again in December, whereupon Nokrashy Pasha was once again appointed Prime Minister on December 10, 1946.

The Funeral of Nokrashy Pasha
Cairo, Dec. 29 (AP) The state funeral of Prime Minister Nokrashy Pasha took place on Wednesday morning in Cairo. The funeral procession passed through the city center to a mosque, where a service was held. Then followed the transfer of the body to the mausoleum that was built for the former Prime Minister Ahmed Maher Pasha, who was also assassinated in February 1945. The inauguration of the mausoleum was to take place shortly. The body of Ahmed Maher Pasha was brought there at night so that the two friends and comrades-in-arms could rest side by side.

The press points to the parallel careers of these two statesmen, who always worked for national liberation, both had to endure exile and prison, and finally, while in office as prime ministers, were assassinated by young fanatics.

Statements of the Assassin
Cairo, Dec. 29 (AP) The assassin of Nokrashy Pasha stated during interrogation that the assassination was a protest against the policy of the Prime Minister. (Ban of the "Muslim Brotherhood," policy in Sudan and Palestine.) The assassin is the son of a former official of the Ministry of the Interior; he has been a member of the "Muslim Brotherhood" organization for several years. His studies at the Veterinary Medical Faculty were made possible by a scholarship that had been personally granted to him by Nokrashy Pasha.

In a desk drawer of the assassinated Prime Minister, a stack of threatening letters was found that Nokrashy Pasha had received and about which he had not even ordered an investigation.

Since a state of siege has been in effect in Egypt since the outbreak of the war with Palestine, the assassin will be sentenced by a military court.

The Gap

It is about the gap that, unfortunately! widens between Swiss Germans and Swiss Romans. It suggests to Mr. E. Juillerat, at the "Jura" in Porrentruy, these useful reflections aimed at proposing a solution:
We believe that a favorable reaction would be the development of a very precise and especially clear federal program, one that is not just verbal. Indeed, words no longer have much weight... given the contempt we see rising within parliamentary assemblies, where Romans simply claim to defend their legitimate cantonal freedoms.
If we want to avoid worsening the malaise, expanding this gap in a way that harms the spirit of concord at a time when 11 seems necessary, action is required.
Concord? It will not be established through protests. We cannot achieve it by capitulation, because what is meaningful in Swiss Romanism, the dignity of patriotism and just pride, Jamais will ever be included.
Unfortunately, there will be opportunists eager to sell their rights—both personal and those of their fellow citizens—to substantial advantages. Not only that, but also the teachings of scholars followed by loyal followers who will make traditions and real principles of law cheap to applaud anything that promotes unification, which poses a danger to Switzerland.
But the majority of Romans, if properly guided, if shown clearly the positions to defend, the heritage to preserve, will not hesitate to say: "Halt there!" To a majority, a Federal Council lacking the true understanding of what it deserves and the rights granted by the constitution itself.
Therefore, 11 It is now essential to ensure cohesion, to set up a plan absolutely free from attacks, leaving bridges intact, but inspired by a firm will against unification that would lead to tyranny. Already now, while the majority senses the country threatened by mysterious foreigners, it shows only stubbornness provoking the most painful consequences.
What would happen if all the safeguards that still hold the federalism in place were destroyed?
That the Roman minority should then energetically act not only for their rights but for the country itself. It is time.
A single representative of the people
In a statement to the press, the Swiss National Action recalled the singular past of Humbert-Droz, who recently joined the Swiss Parliament.
This man, whom we have just judged fit to sit in the Swiss Parliament, played a leading role at the sixth International Communist Congress in 1928. He worked with the sinister Boukharine, reporting for the session where he was elected the "Presidium" of the Komintern.
He presented candidates on behalf of the Komintern leadership and was even nominated to join them. Until the end of 1928, Humbert-Droz was one of those in view for leading the Komintern. He fell out of favor with Boukharine, Ryckoff and Tomsky under the pretext of having "deviated to the right." Both were executed in 1938; Tomsky committed suicide.
In a later letter addressed to the Komintern, Humbert-Droz admitted humbly that the Presidium had "reasoned" to condemn his December 1928 statement as opportunistic hypocrisy and an insult to the International Communist movement. Better still: on October 19, 1930, he fully acknowledged the complete defeat of the direction.
The conclusion of his honorable apology—if we can call it that—was stated as follows: "I declare to the Presidium that I will cease all ideological opposition and, from now on, I will apply its policy not only by discipline but fundamentally convinced that it is the only possible, revolutionary and, consequently, just path available."
This statement provides irrefutable proof of the servility of Dubois-Droz toward Stalin, whom he would now carry out all orders. The Komintern leaders, certain of his loyalty, sent him back to Switzerland to discipline the Communist party and perfect its revolutionary action. Investing in this mission of trust, Humbert-Droz proved himself equally submissive to Moscow.
He humbly accepted the admonitions from foreign masters and carried out all orders. When his former comrades and fellow members of the Russian Communist Party were savagely tortured and executed by Stalin, Humbert-Droz approved the tyrant and published in the press articles praising the massacre perpetrators in Moscow.
These revelations, which every Swiss must reflect on, are borrowed from the "Correspondence International" of 15 May 1928 and 8 December 1930.
The Romania and Germans of the Sudetenland
It is interesting to see how Romania, one of the countries of the Entente, reacts to the German action in Czechoslovakia. "Romanian independence reflects Mr. Henlein's speech at the Karlsbad Congress and what follows: "
Henlein's intentions, as they appear in his Karlsbad speech, aim to put into practice the revaluation of all values with the help of Prague's government. First, by internal decomposition, he wants Czechoslovakia to abandon its foreign policy. Its comparison with Switzerland cannot be made. There are no internal conflicts in this country, and its neutrality policy cannot force it to give up anything regarding a neighboring state. All this suggests that Henlein is an idealist despite himself who wants his homeland a paradise.
But if he believes poets and philosophers, he is merely an executor of others' ideas.
On the other hand, in the old State Secretary's office, "Timpul," we read under the title: "From Guillaume Tell to Henlein," the following article:
Mr. Henlein asks more than a legal status; this, naturally within the loyal Czech government, but already in the framework of the centralized state organization, prepares for it. Mr. Henlein demands a federal state, following Switzerland's example, so an entirely new political and not legal order. But, a Swiss-Almanac is above all a citizen of a federated state. His national ideal is freedom and independence of Switzerland. This good, inherited from his ancestors, must be defended against all.
There is no idea more foreign to a Swiss citizen of a four-language federal state than the idea of race. This Idea would mean the death of a federal state. But, Mr. Henlein wants a state that would be federal like Switzerland and racist like Germany. He asks for a new state policy favorable to the "Drang nach Osten" of the Reich. The minority would be autonomous, while the majority would be forced into totalitarian politics by the minority.
In Henlein's "Switzerland," the Ijchapeau de Gessler still exists and Guillaume Tell has not yet appeared... For us, who pay close attention to the expansion of Germany towards the east, Henlein's speech is especially significant.
Our friendly thought now is for this country that does not provoke anyone, which desires peace and, despite everything, is forced to defend with all its will the idea of its political and economic independence: Czechoslovakia."

September hat den Beweis geliefert, daß das Luxemburger Volk zur Freiheit und Selbstständigkeit erwacht ist, und daß eine neue Zeit für unser Land und Volk angebrochen ist. Für wen die Zukunft des Landes ist, kann dem, der mit Aufmerksamkeit die Ereignisse dieser Tage beobachtet hat, nicht mehr zweifelhaft sein. Die immense Majorität des Luxemburger Volkes ist gut, ist kerngesund, und ist des Regimentes, das bisher das Volk unterdrückt hat, übersatt und müde. Die Richtung, welche im Luxemburger Wort vertreten wird, vereinigt alle wahrhaft conservativen Elemente in sich; dort sind alle wirklich gemäßigten und besonnenen Elemente vertreten, und das lange in Unmündigkeit und Unterdrückung gehaltene Volk hat begonnen, sich zur Freiheit und Selbstständigkeit zu erheben.

Die Freunde des Bürokratismus haben versucht, das Luxemburger Wort als Organ einer klerikalen Partei auszuschreien. Dasselbe hat aber nie einseitige klerikale Prinzipien vertreten, es hat alle wahrhaft conservativen Elemente zu sammeln und zu beschützen sich bemüht, und sich immer als die eigentliche Schutzwehr gegen die Revolution und die sociale Auflösung betrachtet. Noch jüngst hat es durch die Aufstellung seiner Wahllisten den Beweis geliefert, daß es keine ausschließlich klerikalen Zwecke verfolgt, sondern daß es nur dem Despotismus einer Seits, und der Anarchie anderer Seits zu wehren strebt. Nie hat es mit einer zweideutigen Partei gemeinschaftliche Sache gemacht, um ein nächstes Ziel zu erreichen, sondern hat, selbst augenblicklichen Vortheil verschmähend, festgehalten an seinen unumstößlichen Prinzipien, anknüpfend an die Geschichte einer besseren Vergangenheit, der Entwickelung einer freieren und glücklicheren Zukunft getrost entgegensehend. Daß die Zukunft für uns ist, beweiset der Ausfall der Wahlen. Fast überall erhielten bei der ersten Abstimmung die vom Luxemburger Centralwahlcomite aufgestellten Candidaten die große Mehrheit der Stimmen, ein Beweis, daß die große Mehrheit der Bevölkerung für uns ist. Und gingen auch bei der zweiten Abstimmung manche Candidaten wieder verloren, wie in Echternach Gierang und Dieschburg, in Wiltz Neumann, in Grevenmachern Kuborn, so ist dennoch das Gesammtergebnis der Wahlen ein erfreuliches zu nennen. Dagegen hat die Partei der Regierung fast überall eine entschiedene Niederlage erlitten, und ihre Hauptvertreter, wie Ledure, Macher, Wellenstein, Lafontaine, Brasseur u. a. fielen meistens gerade deshalb, weil sie Männer der Regierung waren, beim Volke durch. Zu Remich hat die entschiedenste Opposition gegen die Regierung vollständig und aufs glänzendste gesiegt. Zu Esch a. A. haben die außerordentlichsten Anstrengungen Motte's nicht vermocht, den Herren Lafontaine und Würth-Paquet den Sieg zu verschaffen. Letzterer fiel noch in der Ballotage gegen den Priester und Professor Müller (nicht zu verwechseln mit dem Direktor Müller im Athenäum) mit großer Stimmenmehrheit durch. Document (publication date: 1920-07-08): RAWLEY AGAIN

I haven’t been satisfied since I left Cookeville until now. It seemed like I was almost lost, as I stayed in Gainesboro about 18 months or 2 years. There is plenty of money in Jackson County and it is a very rich county. They raise plenty of corn, wheat, hogs and cattle. You can’t beat it for good stock. It has some mighty good people in it. I was born and raised in Gainesboro. It is not like it used to be. It is too slow for D. A.

Main Street in Cookeville looks like Broad Street in Nashville, there is so much business going on here, and if you want a good school for your children here is the place for them as they have good schools, and plenty of churches and Sunday schools, and the best teachers that can be found. They are up on the job in any branch you wish to study.

If you want a house pattern just come here and you can get everything you want in the building line—cement, lime, brick or any stuff you may need in the way of building material.

The Cookeville Roller Mills furnish this place with the best flour, as Mr. Pleas Farley has the best miller that can be found; Mr. Farley is a mighty nice, clever man and handles all kinds of feed stuff. They are up-to-date in that line, wide-awake, and ready to wait on you.

When you are in town just call around at the Midway Barber Shop and take a peek at my place, and get a good haircut for 25¢, or any other kind of barber work you may need day or night; and take a look at Jim Carlen and Mansfield Judd playing checkers. So, if you want to learn any fresh news just call around at D. A. Rawley’s place and you can find it out. If I don’t know, someone will be here to tell you, as they are always posted, and I am, too.

If you want to make a flying trip anywhere on the dirt road, Cookeville is the place to come to hire a car. Good roads and drivers who know the roads. W. W. Brown is always ready, and Jim Koffmeister is too. The latter has a nice garage and is ready to do any kind of work you may need on your car. Frank Shirley runs a car. He is hard to turn down and is a good driver and safe to ride behind. These men don’t want to charge you out of reason. So when you want to go anywhere just fall off at Cookeville.

Well, I was on the square the other day and stopped in Maddux & Massa’s store and found a nice stock of goods. Bob Lee Maddux is a hustler. This store is “on the square” and will treat you right. They have anything you need in the way of clothing and shoes at reasonable prices. Just call around and see if they are not right on the dot.

Well, one of Alfred Smith’s little girls was at my shop to get her hair cut; she is a mighty nice, sweet little girl. Alfred Smith has as nice a family as anybody. I have been at his house and always found Mrs. Smith and Alfred mighty clever people and glad to see you. Alfred is a man who looks after his family and keeps them plenty to eat and wear, and he is a man who always paid his debts. I am sorry to know he is in the trouble he is accused of. There are lots of good men now in trouble serving another man’s time out.

There is no nicer lady than Velda Smith, as I have known her for years. She was raised by good parents, and so was Alfred. That is what I have to say about Alfred Smith and family. What I said in my other letter about whiskey I did not have reference to Alfred, as I have made and sold whiskey and always got the worst end of it. I am as afraid of whiskey as a copperhead.

I met the chief of police the other day and had a chat with him. He tells me the town is getting along fine. Jim Loftis is a fine man and makes a good chief. He treats all alike. Bill Dabbs and Bud Choat are the night police. Dabbs would tackle a lion as quick as he would a man, but that is what it takes to be a policeman.

If you want a good painter, one who can do any kind of painting you might need, come to Cookeville and I will find them for you; and carpenters the same, and bricklayers too—the best anywhere.

Cookeville is the best all around town you can find, and far above the average for its size. Since I came back I notice several new buildings going up. This place is high, clean, and healthy and the people keep it that way.

Mr. Carlen has built a mighty nice concrete walk.

Well, the soldiers going to school here have a 12 day vacation. They are all mighty nice boys and fine company, as I do lots of work for them.

If you want a nice, fresh mess of steak, or other meats or groceries, go to Wilhite & Foutch Bros., as they know how to cut meat, and have a nice, sanitary shop.

If you want the best little paper printed in the United States just subscribe for the Putnam County Herald.

Does anyone want to buy a nice 4-year old Jersey cow and young calf? The cow will give more milk and make more butter than any I ever owned. She is nice, clean and smooth. Also I have a nice saddle horse for sale; good in harness; is 7 years old with 2 good eyes, and is round and sound. Call on the old timer, D. A. RAWLEY. Cookeville.

Document (publication date: 1938-05-11): Le fossé  
Il s'agit du fossé qui, hélas ! se creuse entre Suisses allemands et Suisses romands. Il suggère à M. E. Juillerat, au « Jura » de Porrentruy, ces utiles réflexions tendant à proposer un remède :  
Nous croyons qu'une heureuse réaction serait la mise au point d'un programme fédéraliste très précis et surtout très clair, programme qui ne serait pas seulement verbal. Les mots, en effet, n'ont plus de portée... étant donné le mépris que l'on constate lorsque s'élèvent, dans les assemblées parlementaires, des voix romandes revendiquant simplement la sauvegarde des légitimes libertés cantonales.  
Si l'on veut éviter l'aggravation du malaise, l'élargissement d'un fossé de nature à nuire au bon esprit de concorde au moment où il s'avère si nécessaire, il faut agir.  
La concorde ? Elle ne s'établira pas sur des brimades. On ne pourra l'obtenir au moyen d'une capitulation, car tout ce qui a, en Suisse romande, le sens de la dignité patriotique et d'une juste fierté, n'y souscrira jamais.  
Malheureusement il y aura des courtisans avides et disposés à vendre, contre le plat de lentilles d'avantages substantiels, non seulement leurs droits, mais ceux de leurs concitoyens. Il y aura aussi des doctrinaires suivis par des fidèles qui feront bon marché des traditions, des véritables principes du droit pour applaudir à tout ce qui favorise une unification constituant un péril pour la Suisse.  
Mais la masse des Romands, si elle est bien guidée, si on lui montre nettement les positions à défendre, le patrimoine à conserver, n'hésitera pas à dire une bonne fois : halte-là ! à une majorité, à un Conseil fédéral n'ayant pas la juste notion des égards qu'elle mérite et des droits que lui confère la charte même du pays.  
Donc il importe maintenant d'assurer la cohésion, de fixer, d'établir un plan d'action absolument exempt de sottes attaques, laissant les ponts intacts, mais inspiré d'une volonté fermement résolue contre une unification qui aboutirait à une tyrannie. Déjà maintenant, alors que la majorité sent le pays menacé par les mystiques étrangères, elle ne sait faire montre que d'une intransigeance provoquant les plus douloureux froissements.  
Qu'en serait-il dès le moment où toutes les digues que maintient encore le fédéralisme auraient été sapées ?  
Que la minorité romande agisse donc énergiquement pour sauver non seulement ses droits mais le pays lui-même. Il est temps.

Un singulier représentant du peuple  
Dans un communiqué à la presse, l'Action nationale suisse rappelle le singulier passé de Humbert-Droz, qui vient d'accéder au Conseil national.  
Cet homme, que l'on vient de juger digne de siéger au Parlement suisse, a joué un rôle de tout premier plan au sixième congrès de l'Internationale communiste, en 1928. Il fut, avec le sinistre Boukharine, rapporteur de la séance où fut élu le « Présidium » du Komintern. Il y a présenté les candidats au nom de la direction du Komintern et a été lui-même désigné pour en faire partie. Il y déploya une grande activité jusqu'à la fin de l'année 1928. À la neuvième session du comité exécutif de l'Internationale communiste, il fut chargé du rapport, d'une importance toute particulière, sur la question syndicale.  
Jusqu'à la fin de 1928, Humbert-Droz fut donc l'un des hommes en vue de la direction du Komintern. Il tomba ensuite en disgrâce, avec Boukharine, Rykov et Tomsky, sous prétexte d'avoir « dévié à droite ». Les deux premiers ont été fusillés en 1938 ; Tomsky s'était suicidé.  
Dans une lettre ultérieure, adressée au Komintern, Humbert-Droz reconnut humblement que le Présidium avait eu « raison de condamner sa déclaration de décembre 1928 comme hypocritement opportuniste et comme étant une attaque indigne contre l'Internationale communiste ». Bien mieux : le 19 octobre 1930, Humbert-Droz fit acte de soumission complète envers la direction du Komintern. La conclusion de son amende honorable — si l'on peut dire — est formulée comme suit : « Je déclare au Présidium que je cesse toute opposition idéologique et que, dorénavant, j'appliquerai sa politique non seulement par discipline, mais foncièrement convaincu qu'elle est la seule possible, la seule révolutionnaire et, par conséquent, la seule juste dans la situation présente ».  
Cette déclaration fournit la preuve irréfutable de la servilité de Humbert-Droz envers Staline, dont il exécutera désormais tous les ordres. Les chefs du Komintern, sûrs de sa fidélité, le renvoyèrent en Suisse pour y discipliner le parti communiste et perfectionner son action révolutionnaire. Investi de cette mission de confiance, Humbert-Droz fit preuve de la même soumission à Moscou. Il accepte humblement les admonestations de ses maîtres étrangers et en exécute tous les ordres. Nommé secrétaire du parti, il s'applique à mettre en pratique les décisions du congrès de l'Internationale communiste, organise des cours pour la formation d'agents de propagande et travaille de toutes ses forces à l'établissement d'un Front populaire suisse. Lorsque ses anciens amis et chefs du parti communiste russe sont sauvagement torturés et exécutés par Staline, Humbert-Droz approuve le tyran et fait publier dans la presse du parti des articles à la gloire des massacreurs de Moscou.  
Ces révélations, que tout Suisse se doit de méditer, sont empruntées à la « Correspondance Internationale » des 15 mai 1928 et 8 décembre 1930.

La Roumanie et les Allemands des Sudètes  
Il est intéressant de voir comment la Roumanie, un des pays de la Petite-Entente, réagit en face de l'agitation allemande en Tchécoslovaquie. « L'Indépendance roumaine » commente le discours de M. Henlein au congrès du parti des Allemands des Sudètes à Karlsbad et écrit ce qui suit :  
Les intentions de M. Henlein, telles qu'elles apparaissent dans son discours de Karlsbad, ont pour but de mettre en pratique l'enseignement de Nietzsche sur la revalorisation de toutes les valeurs et cela avec l'aide du gouvernement de Prague. Tout d'abord, par une décomposition intérieure, il désire faire renoncer la Tchécoslovaquie à sa politique extérieure propre. Sa comparaison avec la Suisse ne peut se faire. D'une part, il n'y a pas de conflits intérieurs dans ce pays et, d'autre part, la politique de neutralité de ce pays ne peut l'obliger de renoncer à quoi que ce soit à l'égard d'un État voisin. Tout fait croire que M. Henlein est un idéaliste malgré lui qui veut faire de sa patrie un paradis. Mais s'il croit aux poètes et aux philosophes, il n'est qu'un exécuteur des idées des autres.  
D'autre part, dans l'organe de l'ancien sous-secrétaire d'État Gafenco, « Timpul », nous lisons, sous le titre : « De Guillaume Tell à Henlein », l'article suivant :  
M. Henlein demande plus qu'un statut juridique unifié, ce que d'ailleurs le gouvernement tchécoslovaque en toute loyauté, mais naturellement dans le cadre de l'organisation juridique de l'État centralisé, prépare déjà. M. Henlein demande un État fédératif, selon l'exemple de la Suisse, donc un nouvel ordre politique et non juridique. Mais, un Suisse alémanique est avant tout un citoyen de la Suisse. Son idéal national est la liberté et l'indépendance de la Suisse. Ce bien, hérité de ses ancêtres, il est décidé de le défendre contre tous. Il n'y a pas d'idée qui serait plus étrangère à un Suisse, citoyen d'un État fédératif à quatre langues que l'idée de race. Cette idée serait la mort d'un État fédératif. Mais, M. Henlein veut un État qui serait fédératif comme la Suisse et raciste comme l'Allemagne. Il demande que le nouvel État fasse une politique qui soit favorable au « Drang nach Osten » du Reich. La minorité serait autonome, tandis que la majorité serait obligée de faire la politique totalitaire de la minorité.  
Dans « la Suisse » de Henlein, le chapeau de Gessler existe encore et Guillaume Tell n'a pas encore fait son apparition... Pour nous, qui suivons avec toute l'attention nécessaire l'expansion allemande vers l'est, le discours de M. Henlein est spécialement significatif.  
Notre pensée amicale est maintenant pour ce pays qui ne provoque personne, qui désire la paix et qui, malgré tout, est forcé de défendre avec toute la volonté l'idée de son indépendance politique et économique : la Tchécoslovaquie.

Document (publication date: 1886-06-22): Neueste Mittheilungen. Verantwortlicher Herausgeber: Dr. H. Klee. V. Jahrgang. Berlin, Dienstag, den 22. Juni 1886. No. 67.

Die Wiederaufnahme der parlamentarischen Arbeiten

Der Reichstag nimmt nach längerer Pause seine Arbeiten am 25. Juni wieder auf; das Abgeordnetenhaus ist am 22. Juni zur Erledigung noch rückständiger Arbeiten wie zur Beschlußfassung über den inzwischen vorgelegten Entwurf betreffs der Unterstützung der durch die letzten Weichselüberschwemmungen Geschädigten zusammengetreten. Die Arbeiten der letztgenannten Körperschaft werden sich voraussichtlich schnell abwickeln, und mit der zweiten vom Herrenhause vorzunehmenden Abstimmung über das Lehrer-Anstellungsgesetz wird die Session des Landtags geschlossen werden können.

Bezüglich der Dauer der Session des Reichstags liegen die Verhältnisse nicht so klar. Freilich, wenn man die freisinnigen Blätter liest, wäre das Sachverhältnis ganz einfach: der Reichstag soll kurzer Hand die ihm noch verbliebenen oder neu vorgelegten Entwürfe zurückweisen und, wenn nichts anderes hilft, durch parlamentarische Arbeitseinstellung den alsbaldigen Schluß der Session herbeiführen. Das kennzeichnet so recht die Art, wie auf oppositioneller Seite Politik gemacht wird: man fragt nicht nach den Interessen des Landes, sondern nach denen der Partei oder des einzelnen Individuums, denen man — bewußt oder unbewußt — den Vorzug gibt, weil man glaubt, stets den Interessen der Regierung, und nicht denen des Landes gegenüberzustehen. Indeß diese Auffassung, die nur zu sehr an die Zeit der politischen Kinderschuhe erinnert, sollte doch angesichts der hohen Bedeutung der Fragen, zu deren Entscheidung der Reichstag nunmehr wieder zusammengetreten ist, von Allen, die nicht blind sein wollen, als völlig unhaltbar erkannt werden.

Es handelt sich jetzt in erster Linie darum, die Frage der Branntweinbesteuerung, für welche die Commission keine Lösung gefunden hat, in das rechte Geleis zu bringen. Es wäre in der That ein Armuthszeugniß, wenn die über die Majorität verfügenden Parteien, welche die Nothwendigkeit der Branntweinsteuererhöhung aus finanziellen und sittlichen Gründen anerkennen und zugleich auch von der Nothwendigkeit einer entsprechenden Berücksichtigung der landwirthschaftlichen Interessen überzeugt sind, und von denen jede für sich ein gewisses Angebot zur Bethätigung ihrer Bereitwilligkeit gemacht hat, sich im Plenum ebensowenig wie in der Commission über ein angemessenes positives Ergebniß einigen könnten, sondern den grundsätzlichen Gegnern, welche von vornherein die Reform zum Scheitern bringen wollten und bis auf den heutigen Tag nicht müde wurden, derselben unter Anwendung aller möglichen und unmöglichen Mittel Hindernisse zu bereiten, in die Hände arbeiten wollten. Es ist doch wohl zu erwarten, daß diese Parteien den Freisinnigen keine Gelegenheit geben werden, sich ins Fäustchen zu lachen, sondern vor Allem, der Pflichten gegen das Land eingedenk, die Steuerfrage sachlich und gründlich beraten und für die Befriedigung der schon seit langer Zeit genügend bekannten und berechtigten Bedürfnisse des Reichs, der Einzelstaaten und Gemeinden neue Einnahmequellen erschließen.

Neben der Branntweinsteuerfrage wird den Reichstag auch noch das Gesetz über die Errichtung eines Seminars für orientalische Sprachen und ein Gesetz über die Versorgung der Hinterbliebenen des Reichsheeres und der Kaiserlichen Marine beschäftigen. Das erstere ist ein Ausfluß der durch die Kolonialpolitik veränderten Weltstellung Deutschlands, dem alle Parteien wohl Rechnung tragen werden, das andere eine Pflicht der Gerechtigkeit gegen die Angehörigen der Armee und Marine, welche sich in dieser Beziehung noch immer nicht in der Lage befinden, wie die Civilbeamten. Daß auch hier wieder den besonderen Verhältnissen der Armee Rechnung zu tragen sein wird, ist selbstverständlich, ebenso selbstverständlich aber auch, daß die Opposition hier wieder ihre Hebel einsetzen wird. Die Gefahr, daß der Schluß der Session unfruchtbar verlaufen wird, ist vorhanden, wenn nicht die Konservativen, das Centrum und die Nationalliberalen die Verpflichtung empfinden werden, den Freisinnigen einen Strich durch die Rechnung zu machen, welche diese für den Schluß der Session aufgestellt haben.

Zwei Jahre Colonialpolitik

Am 23. Juni sind es zwei Jahre, daß der Reichskanzler Fürst Bismarck bei Gelegenheit der Berathung der damals eingebrachten ersten Post-Dampfervorlage der Budgetcommission die Mittheilung machte, daß die Lüderitz'schen Erwerbungen in Südafrika ohne Widerspruch Englands unter deutschen Schutz gestellt seien. À LA VEILLE DU SCRUTIN  
(Correspondance particulière)  

Berne, le 24 octobre.  

Nous avons longuement exposé, lundi, les aspects généraux de la lutte ardente qui se prépare et montré combien les divergences de tendances et de nuances se fondaient, au sein des partis bourgeois ou nationaux, pour concentrer offensive et défensive sur un seul front : celui de l'ordre social et de la démocratie...  

Les quelques jours qui se sont écoulés depuis, journées fertiles en agitations électorales, saturées de déclamations politiques et submergées de tracts incendiaires, n'ont fait qu'affermir les volontés nationales et renforcer toutes les positions bourgeoises contre l'adversaire commun : l'extrême-gauche.  

Dans les milieux politiques fédéraux, on se montre, avec raison pensons-nous, optimistes quant à l'issue de la grande bataille engagée et soit les conseillers fédéraux radicaux, soit leurs collègues catholiques, s'attendent à un renforcement de leurs positions respectives par le succès partiel de leurs troupes. On escompte, soit une avance radicale à Berne, Zurich, Saint-Gall, Grisons, soit une avance conservatrice à Zurich, Schwytz, peut-être Saint-Gall et peut-être Valais. Quel que soit le succès de la liste socialiste, on s'accorde généralement à prévoir qu'il ne suffira pas à procurer aux disciples de Marx le gros succès moral de conquérir la majorité relative au Parlement. La masse électorale, dans son ensemble, a fini par comprendre qu'en coupant les racines et en entamant le tronc de l'arbre économique national, on dessécherait fatalement, finalement, branches, feuilles et fruits...  

Bâle-Ville députait à Berne quatre bourgeois et trois extrémistes. Un parti « évangélique » intervient, cette fois, dans la mêlée et a refusé l'apparentement avec les autres partis nationaux. Cette attitude étrange n'est pas sans causer des inquiétudes sur l'issue du scrutin dans la grande ville du Rhin et l'on craint que l'évangélisme n'y serve de tremplin aux moscoutaires, ce qui serait à déplorer vivement.  

Bâle-Campagne est fertile en dissidents et en brouillons. On craint que les fantaisies électorales de certains pêcheurs en eau trouble n'y soient fatales aux radicaux.  

Pas de changement prévu à Soleure, qui envoie à Berne 3 radicaux, 2 catholiques et 2 socialistes, ni en Argovie, dont la députation actuelle comporte 3 catholiques, 3 paysans, 4 socialistes et 2 radicaux, ni au Tessin, qui se complaît à remanier sans cesse le personnel de ses délégations sans modifier l'importance numérique des partis représentés.  

Trois enclaves de paix au sein de la fournaise électorale : Glaris, heureux pays, qui réélit tacitement son excellent député radical ; Appenzell Extérieures, terre de félicité, qui proclame élus sans combat d'aucune sorte ses deux radicaux et son socialiste ; et enfin Appenzell Intérieur, îlot classique de l'inaltérable fédéralisme, qui refuse imperturbablement « tout ce qui vient de Berne » et qui juge inutile de déranger ses électeurs pour si peu de chose.  

À Neuchâtel, on assiste sans regret à l'effritement lamentable de la liste catholique, absurdité d'inspiration malencontreuse et d'importation étrangère, et l'on escompte que cette dissidence fâcheuse ne nuira pas, en compte final, à la cause nationale.  

À Fribourg, la lutte est extrêmement vive, grâce à l'entrée en scène, pour la première fois, d'un parti « paysans, artisans et bourgeois ». Cette nouvelle constellation électorale pourrait bien enregistrer d'emblée un premier succès, mais nul ne peut prédire si le siège conquis sera enlevé au parti majoritaire ou aux radicaux.  

Les choses semblent devoir se passer beaucoup plus calmement dans le canton de Vaud, où aucun changement notable n'est prévu, et à Genève, où l'on s'attend généralement à un déchet démocrate en faveur du parti de défense économique. C'est M. de Rabours que tous livrent d'avance au fatal couperet de la guillotine sèche. Si pareille prédiction devait se vérifier exacte, le Parlement perdrait une de ses figures les plus sympathiques et l'un de ses meilleurs orateurs, à un moment où les disciples de Démosthène, à Berne, se comptent presque sur les doigts !... B.

Document (publication date: 1898-05-02): Rudolf Koller Jubilee Exhibition in Zurich.

On Sunday, the opening of the Rudolf Koller Jubilee Exhibition took place ceremoniously in the grand hall of the Stock Exchange. The board and various committees of the Zurich Art Society had assembled at 10 a.m. On behalf of the special committee entrusted with organizing the Koller exhibition, City Architect Gull handed over the completed exhibition to the board. The president of the Art Society, Dr. Carl von Muralt, accepted the exhibition on behalf of the board and expressed heartfelt thanks to all members who had contributed to its completion. The president dedicated warm words to the elderly artist present, in whose honor the exhibition was held. Rudolf Koller, deeply moved, thanked with an emotional voice for the honor bestowed upon him. Thereupon, the exhibition was declared open.

The members of the board and committees then undertook a tour through the splendidly arranged rooms, where feverish activity had prevailed in recent days. The large Stock Exchange hall has been divided into three art cabinets. High curtains separate the individual sections from one another. The arrangement and division of the hall are as tasteful as they are practical and clear. If one begins viewing the works upon entry to the left, one first encounters Koller's works from his earliest period. In the first paintings, one clearly recognizes the influences of his training and sees how the young artist initially engaged with great success in various fields of painting before he managed to define his own creative domain. The paintings are hung approximately in chronological order, and one should always keep to the left during viewing, thus first along the walls on the window side towards Bahnhofstrasse, until reaching the section at the end of the hall, from where, still keeping left, one returns to the entrance, where the paintings from the artist's last period are placed. The final piece is the well-executed oil portrait that Jakob Welti was permitted to design of Rudolf Koller last year.

With this chronological arrangement, one can clearly observe how the artist gradually fought his way to his own independent style, how he increasingly freed himself from any academic template and focused solely on faithful observation of nature, how he simultaneously became more powerful in color, more sovereign in composition, and how he knew more and more how to give his paintings a rich atmospheric content, even filling many with a warm glow of poetic feeling.

Alongside the paintings, among which we find many good old acquaintances but also many valuable pieces that have never been publicly exhibited until now, are studies and sketches, placed whenever possible from the respective period. The rich abundance of these splendid studies from nature gives the exhibition a very distinctive character; it grants us a deep insight into the artistic creation of the master, who studied from nature with an intensity and perseverance like hardly any other. In most of these studies lies a burgeoning elemental force and an unparalleled immediacy. As is well known, long before "plein air painting" became a popular catchphrase, Koller, abandoning the artificial light of the studio, created not only his studies but also finished paintings, genuine "plein air pictures," outdoors. It is particularly interesting at this exhibition to compare the studies with the finished paintings; for example, a whole series of sketches and studies serve as a foil for his well-known picture "The Gotthard Post," which, thanks to the owner's cooperation, is also on view here.

A rich life's work is spread out before us on the color-splashed walls here in a magnificent assembly, unlikely to be achieved a second time. One marvels at this overabundant richness that the strength of a single artist sufficed to create all these works in the brief span of a human life. One may well assert that the grand Stock Exchange hall, which has already served many art exhibitions, has never before housed such a wealth of most delightful artworks. Alongside the smaller pictures and studies extend the expansive surfaces of large-format paintings, in which the artist's powerful individuality could express itself most completely. Up to the height of the hall's gallery, which is festively and picturesquely decorated with splendid old carpets, the pictures are arranged in rows. We find there works in which the artist aimed primarily at decorative effect.

For contemplative viewing, the space is suitably arranged. In the middle of the individual sections, one finds resting benches, before which splendid carpets spread out, where one gladly surrenders to the quiet enjoyment of all the beauty.

Koller's life's work is so extensive that the grand Stock Exchange hall was insufficient to contain the abundance of pictures. In the Artists' House, a small, select elite exhibition of Koller's works is additionally housed, where we particularly have the opportunity to admire a series of the artist's fine hand drawings. The walls of the top-lit hall in the Artists' House are filled with a few major pieces by Koller from his most mature period.

Not enough with that. Since the Artists' House and Stock Exchange hall were insufficient, the exhibition committee requested the artist's permission to also make his studios serve the exhibition enterprise. After some hesitation, Mr. Koller agreed, and thus the public will now have the opportunity to also visit the master's workplace, where he has been active for the greater part of his life. Koller's studios in the beautifully situated country estate at Zurichhorn (Fröhlichstrasse 1, near the tram station) contain a series of interesting studies and pictures, particularly from recent times, and will undoubtedly become the pilgrimage site in the coming weeks to which art lovers and admirers of the artist will journey.

After the Rudolf Koller Jubilee Exhibition was declared open on Sunday morning, a numerous public already crowded into the exhibition rooms, expressing in words of delight their astonishment at the richness and beauty of this collection. Considerable attendance from out of town is also particularly expected.

The richly illustrated exhibition catalog will, as we are informed, appear on Wednesday. Family subscriptions at a reduced price are being issued to members of the Zurich Art Society, which are also valid for family members. For visiting the studios at Zurichhorn, the exhibition visitor receives a special admission ticket free of charge at the cash desk in the Artists' House or in the Stock Exchange, which entitles them to visit Koller's studios.

Stories from Home  
Although a native of Brévine or more precisely of Châtagne, Aicide Matthey de l'Etang (Matthey de la Gouille, as his friends called him) spent most of his life in this Jurassic valley where the Solitaire lived during Sagnes and Gédéon le Contreleyu. This place had been chosen for him on a memorable occasion—one beautiful day, or rather a rather unfortunate evening—when he ventured to ask his wife, the great Uranie Montandon du Ronillet, for help. To her complete surprise, she replied negatively. When he asked for the reasons behind this refusal, she simply said, "He felt too much like an horloger."  
For a while, Alcide scolded himself for disappointment in the Lake of Tailleres, but his good sense reminded him that preservation was important. He spent an hour or two shaking off the dust from his boots and eventually set up his tent at Cœudres, thinking his deep sorrow would seep into the misty hills of Sagne. As a horologist by profession, he was also a passionate forest runner, gathering fruits and mushrooms, collecting rare plants for the herbalist in Geneveys, or amassing curiosities from animal, mineral, and vegetable realms to enrich the village museum—where glowing relics of the good old days gathered, including an autograph from Victor Hugo and weapons from Zanzibar.  
To be frank, Aicide Matthey was a fascinating and original personality, somewhat melancholic and not very sociable, seeing only malice and selfishness in people. He liked to wander alone through the surrounding forests or the _pâturages de Sonmartel or the Mont-Racine, muttering and speculating about people and things. After all that, he was a reliable and compliant man who would never have done harm to a fly.  
One Saturday in late autumn, after finishing his usual duties, he set off toward Mont-Racine around four o'clock, walking the path he knew well and which, straight ahead, led him close to the summit. He walked briskly, scanning the surroundings for anyone who might be lurking nearby—just in case he preferred a longer detour to stay alone. Soon he approached the ridge overlooking the pastures and stopped near three pines to light his pipe.  
After finishing this task, he turned slightly left to climb up the signal point when he spotted a small clearing with something buried there. Intrigued, he leaned against the trees and began examining the unknown. After a few minutes, he paused, then looked at an object in his hands. Five minutes later, he started digging again. Soon after, he dropped his shovel into a white box he pulled out from beneath the earth.  
He opened it without hesitation and found something very light: "Bad sign," he said, shaking his head. Driven by curiosity like an old woman, he opened the box, which contained a folded piece of paper resting on an orchid and a tuft of gold leaves. He read the note aloud:  
"Happy to have a loyal heart returning home."  
In memory of August 28, 1928.  
f. Zélie et Pierrot  
The old boy didn't take long to understand how the young love-struck traveler, coming here in pilgrimage, would revisit the places where, on a beautiful summer Sunday, they spent hours by the sparkling Alps—memory sweet and happy moments he wished the place remembered:  
...we drew a line on the map, our hearts thinking of the blue horizons. Holding his find tightly in his hands, we realized our man was rather embarrassed for having intruded on this secret haven. But his bitterness of sighing would soon return to him; he grumbled:  
'Yes, yes, all this is beautiful—provided it doesn't last long. He thought about writing it down out of fear of being recognized, but he put the object back in its place, wrapped it carefully, and set off again. And as he climbed back up, that phrase kept repeating to him: 'A heart, a loyal heart on your return.' Don't worry about it for nothing.  
Thinking of Zélie and Pierrot, if they ever found their cherished memories, they might never have doubted that a brave knight had disturbed something in the heart of a noble soul. Fade out.'"

Document (publication date: 1868-02-19): **Sixth Year, Issue 8. Provincial Correspondence; February 19, 1868.**

**The Provincial Fund in the House of Lords.**

The House of Lords has justified the confidence recently expressed in this place: in the matter of the Hanoverian Provincial Fund, it has placed the viewpoints of a grand patriotic policy above all other considerations and inclinations and granted the state government its willing and full support for implementing its intentions for the new province. More numerous than usual, the members of the House have declared themselves in favor, and even those who did not oppose the proposed grant in general, but only partially against its amount and form.

The question, which had unexpectedly stirred the political circles so intensely, has thus been led to a satisfactory solution through agreement between the government and both houses of the parliament: for the provincial needs of Hanover, insofar as they were previously satisfied from general state funds, provision is now also made by the state, albeit not, as originally proposed, through the allocation of a separate capital, but through the permanent grant of a fixed annuity. Thus, the benevolent intention of the King for the newly acquired province is fulfilled.

In the earlier discussion of the matter, it was repeatedly emphasized that for the government, it was about fulfilling an explicit royal promise given to the Hanoverian estates. This promise referred, of course (as stressed from another side), initially only to the submission of the draft law to the parliament. Its fulfillment lay not solely in the hands of the government, but also depended on the independent judgment of the state representation. However, the government had to proceed from the confidence that those parties, on which this placed particular weight, would be prepared to support the government, especially in questions that awakened hopes through that promise, and would stand willingly by it in fulfilling those hopes.

In this place, reference had been made to the given promise. The King's expectation has not been disappointed: only temporary unjustified doubts about the significance of the matter could have created a momentary uncertainty about its outcome. After the position of the government had been disseminated, after the question was decided as a question of trust and approval of the overall policy of the government, it could no longer be doubtful that the royal promises for Hanover would find willing fulfillment on the part of the state representation.

The policy, which the House of Lords has now also approved, is a policy of benevolence and justice. The government certainly holds the opinion and intention far from "buying the patriotism of the Hanoverians with money"; but it may well hope, through mildness, justice, and brotherly accommodation for the new provinces, to prepare a ground there on which gradually attachment and patriotic devotion can thrive.

But not only in Hanover, not only in the recently acquired parts of the country is that high-minded policy appreciated: everywhere in Germany and beyond its borders, the attention and recognition of the government and the peoples are directed at Prussia's conduct in the conquered provinces. The most significant voices from South Germany announce just the powerful impression that the firm stance of the government has spread.

As Count Bismarck rightly pointed out, this Hanoverian question could only be correctly judged in connection with Prussia's overall policy. By the House of Lords, through its latest decision, entering anew with full determination for this policy, it has simultaneously increased the confidence that the conservative party, which has hitherto followed the government with full trust and devotion, will continue to find its task and its honor in supporting a government which has achieved and created so much for Prussia and Germany and therefore may claim the trust of the German people in full measure.

**The so-called Hanoverian Legion.**

While the Prussian government shows the greatest and noblest consideration to the former King of Hanover, while on the other hand its care for the new province under the benevolent cooperation of the greater part of the population prepares the ground for a blessed development there, King George and his entourage in Hietzing continue the reprehensible attempts to win a part of his former subjects, mostly from the lowest classes, for the completely hopeless and foolish undertaking of restoring his throne.

At the time when the Luxembourg question threatened to bring about a complication between Germany and France, King George had recruitments for a Hanoverian legion organized in his former country, which was to gather in Holland and march in alliance with the French against their fatherland. When then the Luxembourg affair found a peaceful solution, the gathered crowd of Hanoverians went to Switzerland, where it remained in firm military division and continually received its sustenance from the funds of King George. Through its idle roaming and its arrogance, it often caused annoyance there and was not viewed very kindly by the Swiss population as well as by the cantonal governments.

Recently, this so-called "Hanoverian Legion" went from Switzerland to France, where it first took residence in Alsace, immediately at the German border.

As harmless as this foolish undertaking is, it must nevertheless cause astonishment that an obviously armed crowd of Hanoverian refugees accomplished their relocation from Switzerland to France with the help of Austrian passports and that the same in France, as initially reported, found accommodating reception from the authorities.

The French government has meanwhile taken steps on its part to counter such an interpretation: it has separated the men from the officers and removed the crowd from the German border. The Prussian government has no reason to distrust the friendly intentions of France regarding the further treatment of the matter.

As for Austria, assurance has been given by the government there that the passports for the Hanoverians were issued by the Austrian police authority without the knowledge of the Austrian state government, which, given the large number of passports and the unmistakable political significance of the matter, must certainly appear highly remarkable. The discussions between the Prussian and Austrian governments on this point are still ongoing; it cannot yet be definitively stated whether and to what extent a violation of international law has occurred in the affair.

But this can hardly be doubted: the continuation of such enterprises against Prussia cannot be considered as a sign of a friendly stance towards Prussia. In reference to the conduct of King George, the State Minister von der Heydt has just expressed in the House of Lords that if the hostile attempts of the same persist, if King George assumes a position that is completely in contradiction with the spirit and sense of the treaty concluded with him—if King George abuses the hospitality granted to him for recruiting Prussian subjects for a warlike enterprise—then the government will be obliged to take measures.

No. 7. The Egyptian Prime Minister Mahmoud Fahmy El-Nokrashy Pasha, who was assassinated in Cairo on Monday, belonged, although he was already 60 years old, to the relatively young politicians who only entered the political arena in the last two decades. A former supporter of the Wafd, like virtually all Egyptian politicians, he first came to the fore as Minister of Transport in the second cabinet of Nahas Pasha, which remained in office only from January to June 1930. He held the same office again in the third Nahas cabinet from May 1936. His lively personality made him particularly popular among the young adherents of the party and also brought him closer to his party friend and contemporary Ahmed Maher Pasha, the President of the Chamber of Deputies, from whom he subsequently never parted.

Their parallel careers began in London, when they were both among the thirteen delegates who signed the Anglo-Egyptian treaty in August 1936. After their return to Egypt, they, as younger members of the party, gained the impression that the Wafd had played its last cards in London and thus had no more prospects to offer its followers. This viewpoint was entirely justified at the time; indeed, the actual decline of the Wafd began at that point. For when the Wafd was founded, the sole aim of its program was the conclusion of a treaty with Great Britain that would recognize Egypt's independence. It is known that the Arabic word "Wafd" means nothing other than "Delegation." This treaty was now wrested from the British by Nahas Pasha. The role of the Wafd "Delegation" was thus played out.

In the following months, the leaders of the party, primarily Makram Ebeid and to a lesser extent Nahas, behaved as if they now had a right to the country's lasting gratitude. Squandering of public funds, corruption, and favoritism became widespread. It was managed as if all hope had been abandoned of ever coming to power again later.

In August 1937, the two friends Maher and Nokrashy broke away from the Wafd and together founded a new party, which they named the Saadist Party after the founder of the Wafd, Saad Zaghloul, under the pretext that the party founded by him had not remained true to his spirit. The beginnings were difficult. The new party, however, ultimately prevailed, and when in August 1939 Ali Maher Pasha, the brother of Ahmed, needed their support in forming a new cabinet, he offered its president, Nokrashy, the Ministry of Education.

In June 1940, Ali Maher had to resign due to his pro-Axis leanings under pressure from the British embassy, and Nokrashy was taken over by the Hassan Sabry Pasha cabinet as Minister of the Interior. This extremely important office in wartime could undoubtedly only be entrusted to him in agreement with the English.

The Sabry cabinet remained at the helm for only two months. During the opening of parliament, the prime minister was struck by a heart attack while reading the throne speech. His successor, Hussein Sirry, dispensed with the participation of the Saadists. In February 1942, the Hussein Sirry cabinet was replaced by the last Wafd cabinet under Nahas Pasha. When in October 1944 Lord Killearn and the British government finally had to realize that Nahas Pasha's continued presence in the government endangered their own position, they withdrew their support from him and pressed for the appointment of Ahmed Maher Pasha as his successor, who, as an opponent of Nahas and a pro-British minded politician, was well-regarded both in the palace and at the British embassy. The two Saadist leaders had thereby reached the highest level; they divided the key positions between themselves. Maher kept the Ministry of the Interior for himself, and Nokrashy became Foreign Minister. Thus he had completed the second grade of the "prime ministerial school," for it has almost become a tradition in Egypt that the prime minister, unless he has reached his post via the presidency of the Senate or the Chamber, must have administered one of the three main ministries, namely the Interior, Foreign, or Finance Ministry.

Under Ahmed Maher's leadership, Egyptian policy was steered into British waters. Maher had to pay for this policy with his life after only a few months. Maher Pasha was shot dead on February 24, 1945, by a fanatical nationalist just as he was announcing to parliament Egypt's declaration of war on the Axis powers. For Nokrashy, under such circumstances, it was a difficult task to assume the succession of his friend. After the war, nationalism intensified in Egypt, which Nokrashy attempted to counter. As a realist politician who understood how to accurately assess the power resources of his country, he believed he could wrest concessions from the British through friendship, which they would never grant to declared enemies. Personally, Nokrashy would have gladly done without a revision of the London treaty, clearly recognizing that provisions and clauses only have value if one can force the partner to fulfill its obligations through appropriate means. However, he had to yield to the pressure of the "Eighteen," an advisory committee that the king had brought into being. When he wanted to begin negotiations with London, his government had to give way to the machinations of the opposition. Nokrashy lacked the necessary self-control and calm. This was also evident when in February 1946 he ordered the police to ruthlessly shoot at unarmed student crowds who wanted to cross the Abbas Bridge into the government district. His brutal course of action betrayed not energy, but rather fear.

After Nokrashy Pasha's resignation on February 15, 1946, Ismail Sidky Pasha took over the cabinet, which was supported by Nokrashy, but already had to resign again in December, whereupon Nokrashy Pasha was once again appointed Prime Minister on December 10, 1946.

The Funeral of Nokrashy Pasha
Cairo, Dec. 29 (AP) The state funeral of Prime Minister Nokrashy Pasha took place on Wednesday morning in Cairo. The funeral procession passed through the city center to a mosque, where a service was held. Then followed the transfer of the body to the mausoleum that was built for the former Prime Minister Ahmed Maher Pasha, who was also assassinated in February 1945. The inauguration of the mausoleum was to take place shortly. The body of Ahmed Maher Pasha was brought there at night so that the two friends and comrades-in-arms could rest side by side.

The press points to the parallel careers of these two statesmen, who always worked for national liberation, both had to endure exile and prison, and finally, while in office as prime ministers, were assassinated by young fanatics.

Statements of the Assassin
Cairo, Dec. 29 (AP) The assassin of Nokrashy Pasha stated during interrogation that the assassination was a protest against the policy of the Prime Minister. (Ban of the "Muslim Brotherhood," policy in Sudan and Palestine.) The assassin is the son of a former official of the Ministry of the Interior; he has been a member of the "Muslim Brotherhood" organization for several years. His studies at the Veterinary Medical Faculty were made possible by a scholarship that had been personally granted to him by Nokrashy Pasha.

In a desk drawer of the assassinated Prime Minister, a stack of threatening letters was found that Nokrashy Pasha had received and about which he had not even ordered an investigation.

Since a state of siege has been in effect in Egypt since the outbreak of the war with Palestine, the assassin will be sentenced by a military court.

Document (publication date: 1981-05-13): Proche-Orient : jeux avec le feu  
Pourquoi Syriens et Israéliens menacent-ils soudain de s'affronter dans une guerre risquant d'embraser tout le Proche-Orient ?  
L'explication immédiate est connue : pour aider leurs « protégés » chrétiens de la vallée libanaise de la Bekaa, pilonnés par les Syriens, les Israéliens ont fait donner leur aviation et, au cours d'un raid, le 28 avril dernier, abattu deux hélicoptères damascènes.  
La Syrie a réagi instantanément, installant au Liban quelque 14 batteries de missiles sol-air SAM.  
Israël, estimant que cette implantation mettait en cause la suprématie aérienne dont il bénéficiait depuis plusieurs années au Liban, et bouleversait du coup, en sa défaveur, le délicat équilibre régional, exigea de Damas qu'il retire ses missiles.  
Devant le refus syrien, Israël décida, de l'aveu même du premier ministre Begin, de détruire ces batteries de missiles, le 30 avril dernier, mais y renonça momentanément pour des raisons météorologiques, puis indéfiniment, à la demande instante du général Alexander Haig.  
Cette explication est cependant insuffisante.  
Si Israéliens et Syriens voulaient éviter de s'affronter militairement, il leur serait facile de trouver un compromis.  
Alors, en entretenant la tension entre eux, qu'essaient-ils de dire, et à qui ?  
La réponse est évidente : les deux capitales tentent désespérément d'éveiller l'intérêt des États-Unis, et d'attirer ces derniers dans leur jeu respectif.  
Sur le mode : « Faites quelque chose, arrêtez-nous, ou nous ne répondons plus de rien ».  
Depuis l'élection de Ronald Reagan, les Américains ont montré les dispositions suivantes à l'égard du Proche-Orient : 1) priorité générale à la lutte contre l'expansionnisme soviétique ; 2) priorité régionale aux problèmes du Golfe (sécurité des approvisionnements pétroliers) ; et 3) volonté de mobiliser des ressources considérables pour atteindre ces objectifs.  
Or, jadis, le conflit israélo-arabe était au centre de toute stratégie proche-orientale : les protagonistes du conflit en ont tiré, de longues années durant, d'énormes avantages financiers, militaires et politiques.  
On comprend que l'idée de retomber dans l'ombre, l'oubli, l'indifférence, leur apparaisse aujourd'hui insupportable.  
À travers une menace de guerre que les États-Unis sont appelés à régler comme médiateurs, dans une atmosphère de tension sans cesse changeante, sinusoïdale intensément dramatique, ils ont le sûr instinct de pouvoir retrouver un poids qu'ils étaient en train de perdre.  
Le raisonnement est particulièrement vrai pour Israël qui a vu, il y a quelques semaines, les États-Unis disposés à vendre des radars volants à l'Arabie Saoudite, dans un souci prioritaire de renforcer un front antisoviétique dans la région, et en négligeant de considérer les craintes que cette transaction ne pouvait manquer d'éveiller à Jérusalem.  
La Syrie, quant à elle, a fait savoir à Philip Habib, le médiateur dépêché par Ronald Reagan, que les États-Unis étaient seuls à pouvoir influencer efficacement la politique israélienne.  
Une manière de leur dire : « Voudriez-vous vraiment que nous fussions obligés d'appeler l'URSS à notre aide ? »  
À ce stade, on peut dire que les Américains se sont laissés prendre au piège.  
Cela parce qu'ils sont pleins d'une énergie qui cherche emploi, mais n'ont pas encore de politiques spécifiques, ce qui les rend faciles à manœuvrer.  
L'Amérique roulée dans un bazar oriental !  
Le risque n'est pas négligeable cependant que les acteurs, qui feignent de vouloir s'entr'égorger, se prennent à leur propre jeu, et que le jeu tourne au massacre.
